catalog_quote: 2.4. Stress. Stress rules operate after the rules which insert epenthetic [ə] or [ɨ] and which form glides from high vowels. Primary stress normally falls on the vowel of a monosyllable and on the penultimate vowel of a polysyllable: ... Words containing geminate vowel clusters, however, receive stress on that cluster: ... 'quick' ... 'his chest' ... 'to clean'. Exceptions to these rules have the stressed vowel marked with an acute accent: ... In nouns, every alternate syllable to the left of the primary-stressed vowel, including cases of [ə] or [ɨ] inserted between clustering consonants, receives secondary stress: ... In verbs and adjectives, the initial syllable receives secondary stress, as does each alternate syllable to the right of the initial syllable, except that the syllable preceding the primary-stressed syllable is always unstressed: ... The remarks above apply to the Nɨvhaal…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the Lynch 1982 PDF we hold/text at section 2.4, printed and p.10, exactly as cited. (2) Deciding source: a 1982 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch by the fieldworker (John Lynch) with an explicit stress section including secondary stress and dialect notes; Glottolog lists no other descriptive work, and Lynch 2001 p.5 names Lynch 1982a as the sole source for the language. (3) downloaded now: Lynch 2001 PL-509 (open, sealang) p.9 and p.117 restate for the Tanna languages 'normally penultimate, final if the final vowel is long' — this confirms our weight-sensitive (CVV, right-edge, penult default) coding and is consistent with our note that closed final syllables do not attract stress. sources.citation: Lynch, John. 2001. The linguistic history of Southern Vanuatu. Pacific Linguistics 509. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, Australian National University. 334 pp.
sources.quote: p.9: 'Primary stress is invariably on the penultimate syllable in Erromango. In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.' p.117: daughter languages 'all ... have regular penultimate stress, irrespective of whether the final syllable was open or closed ... Long vowels in final syllables attract stress'. p.5 source table: Southwest Tanna — 'Lynch 1982a'.
sources.locator: sec. 1.5.2 'Vowels, phonotactics and stress', p.9; sec. 4.4.3 'Proto Southern Vanuatu stress', p.117; source table p.5
